Appendix A. Ad Vendors Involved in Discover-Tech’s Ad Operations

Google and Yandex

Google dominates the digital advertising ecosystem in the U.S., Europe, and other regions. It operates a massive ad exchange and systems for ad sellers (Ad Manager, AdSense, AdMob) and ad buyers (Google Ads, DV360). Its “Authorized Buyers” program allows third-party ad vendors to deliver ads by participating in ad auctions on Google’s ad exchange.

Yandex, although much smaller in revenue, similarly dominates the digital advertising ecosystem in Russia and some other regions. It also provides both an ad exchange and systems for ad sellers and buyers.

Beeswax, Owned by Freewheel/Comcast

Beeswax is a major US-based ad buying platform, since 2021 owned by Comcast’s ad platform FreeWheel. It offers a Demand-Side Platform (DSP) that helps advertisers and other ad vendors deliver targeted ads to users by participating in ad auctions. Its “bidder-as-a-service” product is considered highly customizable and imposes fewer restrictions on its clients than other DSPs.

The FreeWheel website states that, by using Beeswax’ ad buying platform rather than other DSPs, clients could “access the full, unfiltered stream of RTB events, in much the same way [they] would if [they] were building a bidder from scratch”. Clients can augment the stream of ad bidding data they receive, for example, by “mapping” users to “rich profiles”, and they can use custom bidding algorithms and targeting attributes.

While this appears to offer great flexibility to clients to an extent that may come close to operating their own DSP, FreeWheel takes care of the integrations with ad exchanges and Supply-Side Platforms (SSPs) that help app and website publishers sell ads. As of July 2026, the FreeWheel website lists integrations with 36 “supply partners” including Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Index Exchange, and many others.

Beeswax is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Beeswax as a certified ad vendor and among its “common” European ad technology partners which Google will use by default when publishers do not set up a custom list of ad vendors. For its ad serving and third-party tracking, Beeswax uses the domain bidr[.]io and the cookie identifier bito (devicedisclosure.json).

Eskimi, a White-Label DSP Based in Lithuania

Eskimi is a digital advertising group based in Lithuania with offices in Greece, Turkey, Japan, United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Nigeria, and Kenya, according to its website, eskimi.com. Its ad buying platform Eskimi DSP, which allows its clients to target 1.5 billion “profiled users” across 60 ad exchanges, according to the company, is also offered as a “white-label” version that “enables agencies, ad networks, and businesses to offer ‘Eskimi DSP’ under their own brand”. Eskimi also provides a data management platform (DMP) that “collects and stores data” it receives from 50 ad exchanges, amounting to two2 billion profiles, according to a 2025 version of the company’s website. Its website and Lithuanian company records show that it is incorporated as “UAB Eskimi”, also known as “UAB Aktyvus sektorius”.

Eskimi is much lesser known than Beeswax. Except for two paid posts, we did not find any articles discussing the company on digital advertising trade press sites like Adweek, Digiday, and AdExchanger. Eskimi was, however, prominently discussed when US-based data broker Datastream Group told U.S. Senator Ron Wyden that Eskimi was the source of 3.6 billion location data records revealing the exact movements of millions of people, including U.S. military and intelligence personnel, as reported in a joint investigation by German netzpolitik.org and other outlets. This investigation has helped spark extensive debates about ad surveillance.

While German netzpolitik.org found several additional links between the analyzed data and the company, Eskimi denied that it was the source of the data. Google told 404 Media that Eskimi is “part of Google’s Authorized Buyer program and must abide by our policies”. It added that it “regularly audits its Authorized Buyers program participants”. Eskimi is closely linked to the location data broker Redmob, which claims to sell data on one billion people across 150 countries according to its website, redmob.io. While Redmob is incorporated in Dubai, netzpolitik.org found that Eskimi and Redmob share the same CEO, who responded to their questions about Eskimi from a Redmob email address.

As of July 2026, Eskimi is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Eskimi as a certified ad vendor and among its European ad technology partners.

Vungle, Liftoff’s SSP, and Ad Exchange

Vungle was a mobile advertising firm that merged with the U.S.-based mobile advertising firm Liftoff, which went public in June 2026. Since the merger, Liftoff offers several Vungle-branded products including a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) named Monetize, which helps app publishers sell ads, and the mobile ad exchange Vungle Exchange, which helps marketers buy ads served in mobile apps.

Both the SSP and the ad exchange rely on the Vungle SDK, which is a piece of advertising and tracking software embedded in many Android, iOS, Amazon, Windows, and Unity apps. The Vungle SDK is embedded in 150,000 mobile apps used by one billion people across 150 countries, which also describes the number of users that can be targeted via the Vungle ad exchange, according to the company.

Guidelines for the Vungle ad exchange contain a rule that asks clients to “refrain from” using the platform for the distribution of “malware, spyware, and files that can harm or gain unauthorized access to a device or user information”. We did not find an explanation of how the company monitors and enforces this rule.

Vungle has been controversially discussed in several papers and reports on mobile tracking and privacy. The Norwegian Consumer Council found in 2020 that Vungle received GPS coordinates and other personal data on users of Grindr and another mobile app, seemingly without a legal basis under the GDPR.

As of July 2026, Liftoff’s “Monetize” and “Vungle Exchange” products are listed as approved TCF ad vendors by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Liftoff’s DSP and Monetize products as certified ad vendors and it lists Liftoff among its “common” European ad technology partners that Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors.

Google has been deeply interconnected with Vungle from its inception. Google Ventures was an investor in Vungle’s seed, series A, and series B funding rounds. The Norwegian Consumer Council pointed out in 2020 that Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob “provides Vungle with access to extra features that allow Vungle to bypass data filters, and thus send more data to its partners than what would ordinarily be possible through Google’s regular advertising tools”. As of July 2026, Liftoff’s Vungle product Monetize is listed among a few “premium bidding partners” in Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob and among a few “ad sources” for AdMob’s advertising services on Android and iOS.

Sunteng, a Chinese SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange

The Chinese digital advertising firm Sunteng provides ad buying and selling services for both advertisers and publishers, as well as a “programmatic marketplace”, i.e. an ad exchange, according to its website, sunteng.com. The site also refers to the company as “Shunfei Technology”. The link to Sunteng’s DSP offering leads site visitors to biddingx.com (“BiddingX”), an entity that promotes itself as China’s largest DSP. Sunteng appears to operate also under the brand Bidex (bidex.cn), which focuses on “overseas programmatic”, i.e. on digital advertising services for non-Chinese clients. We assume that Sunteng, Shunfei, Bidex and BiddingX are part of the same Chinese group of companies with offices in Singapore and the US. Sunteng claims to process 50 billion ad bid requests a day across 10,000 mobile apps and 60 ad vendor partners, and it lists Eskimi as a partner.

As of July 2026, Google lists biddingx.com (“Shunfei Infomation Technology Corporatio” [sic]) as a certified ad vendor. IAB Europe listed bidex.cn (“Sunteng Hong Kong Holdings Limited”) as an approved TCF ad vendor until December 2025 (vendor list).

Xandr, aka Microsoft Advertising

Xandr, formerly known as AppNexus, has long been a major player in digital advertising. After Microsoft acquired it from AT&T in 2022, it became part of Microsoft Advertising in 2023. While Microsoft shut down Xandr’s ad buying system, the “Invest” DSP, in early 2026, it continues to offer Xandr’s ad selling system, the “Monetize” SSP. Ad buyers who used the former Xandr DSP were “handed” to Amazon DSP, according to trade press reporting.

As shown in Section 6, Microsoft’s user ID syncing in the browser via the domain adnxs[.]com, which assigns a Microsoft user ID to people who visit the sites of ad sellers and maps it to user IDs assigned by other ad vendors, appears to remain operational as of June 2026. Xandr has long been operating massive identity databases. In 2020, when Xandr was still owned by AT&T, it reportedly operated an identity graph linking 5 billion identifiers.

As of July 2026, Microsoft’s ad system Xandr is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google’s list of certified ad vendors contains four records for Xandr. Google also lists Xandr among its “common” European ad technology partners which Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors.

Appendix B. Glossary

Adtech vendor, ad vendor. Advertising technology intermediary such as a Demand-Side Platform (DSP), Supply-Side Platform (SSP) (both defined below) or ad exchange.

Ad Slot. Designated space or position on a website or mobile app reserved to display an ad.

Demand-Side Platform (DSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps advertisers buy ad placements across many different websites or mobile apps in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by ad exchanges.

Supply-Side Platform (SSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps publishers of websites or mobile apps sell ad slots in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by an ad exchange, which is often operated by the same ad vendor as the SSP.

Ad Exchange. Automated marketplace operated by an adtech intermediary that hosts real-time auctions which facilitate the selling of ad slots and the buying of ad placements across many publishers, advertisers and intermediaries like DSPs and SSPs. Ad exchanges are often operated by SSPs.

Real-Time Bidding (RTB). Automated high-frequency auctions hosted by ad exchanges where advertisers (or DSPs on their behalf) bid on ad placements offered by website and mobile app publishers (or their SSPs). When a user visits a website or uses an app that sells targeted ads via RTB, the publisher’s SSP initiates a bid request that transmits data about the user and the ad slot to several DSPs, who submit bids on behalf of advertisers. The ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user.

Bid Request. RTB auction record that describes an ad slot and the user who currently visits a website or uses a mobile app. Bid requests are initiated by publishers and sent via an SSP and an ad exchange to several DSPs, which place bids in order to show ads to specific users on behalf of advertisers. Bid requests typically contain personal data about users in order to facilitate targeted advertising.

Mobile Advertising ID (MAID). Unique identifier for a mobile device used for advertising and tracking purposes, assigned by the device’s operating system such as Google Android or Apple iOS. While users can reset or delete mobile ad IDs in the settings, they are activated by default. Advertising and data companies use mobile ad IDs to link user data across contexts and vendors in order to track, follow, profile and target users.

Cookie ID. Unique identifier for a user’s web browser, typically stored and retrieved in the browser by third-party code operated by adtech vendors during website visits.

blocks.html_en: The Online Advertising Ecosystem is Ripe for Abuse

sentences.en: The Online Advertising Ecosystem is Ripe for Abuse

blocks.html_en: When a user sees an ad on an app or a website, it is likely the result of a real-time auction, where advertisers bid on the chance to show that specific user that specific ad. So-called Real-Time Bidding (RTB) auctions, which are hosted on ad exchanges operated by companies including Google, take place hundreds of billions of times a day. In less than a second, the user’s device initiates a bid request, advertisers submit their bids, and the ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Besides an image or video, an online ad can also contain code that runs within the app or browser that shows the ad.

blocks.html_en: Both advertisers and publishers of apps and websites use ad vendors that act as their intermediaries in these auctions. Advertisers typically buy ads via a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), and a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) sells ad inventory on websites and apps.

blocks.html_en: Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem:

sentences.en: Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem:

blocks.html_en: The advertising ecosystem collects a lot of data and enables individual-level targeting: When a publisher of an app or website wishes to show ads, they add code from an SSP to their app or site. This code collects and shares granular information about the user and their device with ad exchanges to solicit bids for the ad slots. This information can include device identifiers and characteristics, precise location, and IP address data, as well as data about the app or website, and specifications about the ad slot. The DSP or advertiser then examines this information and decides whether they wish to bid on the impression in order to show an ad. The auction system is designed to enable targeting single individuals based on their mobile advertising ID, cookie ID, IP address, and other identifiers.

Code run by advertisers, DSPs, SSPs, and other third parties within apps and websites is often referred to as “tags”, “pixels”, “SDKs”, or “third-party tracking” more generally.

blocks.html_en: Exploiting Advertising Tech for Surveillance

sentences.en: Exploiting Advertising Tech for Surveillance

blocks.html_en: The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data can track users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports have uncovered vendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies.

blocks.html_en: Zero-Click Spyware Delivered via Targeted Ads: AdFection

sentences.en: Zero-Click Spyware Delivered via Targeted Ads: AdFection

blocks.html_en: Beyond passive data harvesting, malicious parties can also exploit this infrastructure to target certain individuals based on user data included in ad auctions and then run malicious code on their devices. Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection.

blocks.html_en: A large number of ads placed by Discover-Tech contain a script tag pointing back to what the company refers to as a “NOAS server” (also called a “getAd server”). This tag causes the ad, when rendered, to connect back to Discover-Tech, submit advertising identifiers for the user (either a cookie ID or a mobile ad ID), and automatically execute any JavaScript code returned. The NOAS server decides, apparently based on a combination of the source IP address and the advertising identifiers, whether the target is eligible to receive any JavaScript. If so, then code is returned. If not, a 0-byte response is returned. The NOAS server is a key part of Discover-Tech’s strategy, allowing Discover-Tech to avoid directly sharing malicious code, or even pointers to malicious code, with the companies who serve and display the ads.

blocks.html_en: In this report we provide an overview of the different types of ad abuse facilitated by Discover-Tech, the company’s ad targeting systems and practices, as well as its partners and corporate network.

We then outline their relationships with other mercenary surveillance companies, including advertising intelligence (ADINT) vendor Intelos, and an ADINT vendor we refer to as DARK CARTOGRAPHER, which is building databases linking users’ mobile advertising identifiers to their phone numbers.

blocks.html_en: In Section 5, we analyze where Discover-Tech’s malicious advertisements land. We identified a Discover-Tech server that published almost four billion ad bidding records. We also highlight specific countries and government networks where Discover-Tech’s advertisements had impressions.

blocks.html_en: This section provides the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click spyware attack via targeted ads in the wild: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with mercenary spyware. We refer to this type of attack as AdFection. Using network analysis, infrastructure fingerprinting, and analysis of implant behaviour, we connect Discover-Tech’s infrastructure with the distribution of Candiru’s mercenary spyware.

blocks.html_en: What AdFection Looks Like

sentences.en: What AdFection Looks Like

blocks.html_en: The instances of Candiru AdFection via Discover-Tech ads all share similar characteristics. First, Discover-Tech wins a bid, and one of their ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. The user may see this ad, such as in Figure 4, though in some cases the ad may render in the background.

sentences.en: The instances of Candiru AdFection via Discover-Tech ads all share similar characteristics.
First, Discover-Tech wins a bid, and one of their ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device.
The user may see this ad, such as in Figure 4, though in some cases the ad may render in the background.

blocks.html_en: When the website or app receives the ad, it renders it, requesting JavaScript from a Discover-Tech server embedded within the ad. In most cases, the user who sees the ad is not selected for targeting, and the server will not return any JavaScript to be executed.  Nevertheless, the ad will still gather data from the user’s browser and submit it back to Discover-Tech, which can include cookies set on the webpage including the ad, as well as the device’s public IPv6 address.

blocks.html_en: Confirming the Targeting of Al Jazeera with Candiru Spyware via Discover-Tech Ads

sentences.en: Confirming the Targeting of Al Jazeera with Candiru Spyware via Discover-Tech Ads

blocks.html_en: In 2024 and 2025, international news network Al Jazeera was targeted in a series of zero-click attacks that we link with high confidence to Candiru’s spyware delivered via Discover-Tech’s ads. At least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in these attacks.

sentences.en: In 2024 and 2025, international news network Al Jazeera was targeted in a series of zero-click attacks that we link with high confidence to Candiru’s spyware delivered via Discover-Tech’s ads.
At least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in these attacks.

blocks.html_en: Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Infected devices first show contact with domains from Discover-Tech infrastructure, indicating an ad impression. Next, the devices show connections with a Candiru validator server. The validator server performs an initial check of the device before it is further profiled and infected. Ultimately, an infected device communicates with a Candiru Command and Control (C&C) server. This temporal signature is illustrated by Figure 5.

sentences.en: Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed.
Infected devices first show contact with domains from Discover-Tech infrastructure, indicating an ad impression.
Next, the devices show connections with a Candiru validator server.
The validator server performs an initial check of the device before it is further profiled and infected.
Ultimately, an infected device communicates with a Candiru Command and Control (C&C) server.
This temporal signature is illustrated by Figure 5.

blocks.html_en: 3. Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting Platform

sentences.en: Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting Platform

blocks.html_en: This section examines Controlium, a platform that provides a control-panel style interface allowing mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads” that deliver malware. Discover-Tech published the full source code for Controlium’s frontend on the app’s login page, which allowed us to review and reconstruct the user interface.

sentences.en: This section examines Controlium, a platform that provides a control-panel style interface allowing mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads” that deliver malware.
Discover-Tech published the full source code for Controlium’s frontend on the app’s login page, which allowed us to review and reconstruct the user interface.

blocks.html_en: Discover-Tech provides its customers with access to a platform called Controlium that appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements. Customers can use Controlium to select a user for infection or profiling based on their mobile advertising identifier (iOS or Android), browser identifier (MyDSP or Beeswax cookie ID), and/or IP address. Discover-Tech’s malicious ads (referred to as “controlled ads”) sometimes also contain branding of companies that are closely linked to Discover-Tech, or branding from apparently unwitting third-party companies, including Amazon and AliExpress. We have no evidence that these ads were purchased by Amazon or AliExpress.

sentences.en: Discover-Tech provides its customers with access to a platform called Controlium that appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.

Customers can use Controlium to select a user for infection or profiling based on their mobile advertising identifier (iOS or Android), browser identifier (MyDSP or Beeswax cookie ID), and/or IP address.

Discover-Tech’s malicious ads (referred to as “controlled ads”) sometimes also contain branding of companies that are closely linked to Discover-Tech, or branding from apparently unwitting third-party companies, including Amazon and AliExpress.
We have no evidence that these ads were purchased by Amazon or AliExpress.

blocks.html_en: As is standard for many web apps, the entirety of the source code for the Controlium frontend is included on the app’s login page. We visited the login page in a web browser and saved the page to disk to obtain a copy of the frontend.2 We modified our copy of the code to remove any communication with any external servers, and to reveal all available screens in the UI. We then opened this version in a web browser to explore the app’s user interface.

blocks.html_en: In our analysis of Controlium, we downloaded only publicly accessible resources without circumventing any access controls. Most data associated with Controlium, such as information about Discover-Tech’s customers and their operations, is intentionally protected with an authorization token. However, we were able to obtain data on Controlium user logins from an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’). We also assess that it would have been possible for a hacker to spoof a valid authorization (see below: ‘Authentication Vulnerability’), although we did not test this.

blocks.html_en: Authentication Vulnerability

sentences.en: Authentication Vulnerability

blocks.html_en: While the data associated with Controlium’s customers and their operations are nominally protected with an authorization token, it appears that it would be easy for a hacker to spoof a valid token. We did not attempt to exploit this issue, as we believe doing so would have constituted unauthorized access to Discover-Tech’s systems.

sentences.en: While the data associated with Controlium’s customers and their operations are nominally protected with an authorization token, it appears that it would be easy for a hacker to spoof a valid token.
We did not attempt to exploit this issue, as we believe doing so would have constituted unauthorized access to Discover-Tech’s systems.

blocks.html_en: The underlying issue stems from Discover-Tech’s improper use of Okta’s Auth0 product. When a Controlium customer authenticates with Auth0, a JWT is returned to their browser. This token is digitally signed by Auth0, and contains information about scopes and expiry that the backend server should validate. However, Controlium ignores this token and instead passes a separate user object as a token to the backend server. The user object simply contains unauthenticated metadata about the user, such as their name and email address. Controlium encrypts this information with a secret key published in the Controlium platform.

sentences.en: The underlying issue stems from Discover-Tech’s improper use of Okta’s Auth0 product.
When a Controlium customer authenticates with Auth0, a JWT is returned to their browser.
This token is digitally signed by Auth0, and contains information about scopes and expiry that the backend server should validate.
However, Controlium ignores this token and instead passes a separate user object as a token to the backend server.
The user object simply contains unauthenticated metadata about the user, such as their name and email address.
Controlium encrypts this information with a secret key published in the Controlium platform.

blocks.html_en: Interestingly, the correct code to use the JWT as an authorization token was present within the Controlium platform, but was commented out in lieu of the vulnerable code.

We further delve into this data in Section 4.

blocks.html_en: 4. Discover-Tech’s Links with Mercenary Spyware, ADINT, and Mass Surveillance Vendors

sentences.en: Discover-Tech’s Links with Mercenary Spyware, ADINT, and Mass Surveillance Vendors

blocks.html_en: This section examines links between Discover-Tech and the mercenary spyware companies Candiru and Bindecy. We also illustrate that, beyond facilitating mercenary spyware delivery, Discover-Tech is linked to ADINT firms, including Intelos. Discover-Tech also supports mass-deanonymization of internet and app users by a threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER, which exploits vulnerabilities in mobile networks to unmask users’ phone numbers.

sentences.en: This section examines links between Discover-Tech and the mercenary spyware companies Candiru and Bindecy.
We also illustrate that, beyond facilitating mercenary spyware delivery, Discover-Tech is linked to ADINT firms, including Intelos.

Discover-Tech also supports mass-deanonymization of internet and app users by a threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER, which exploits vulnerabilities in mobile networks to unmask users’ phone numbers.

blocks.html_en: We observed that Discover-Tech sends encrypted ad impression data to Candiru using Controlium’s “Ad URL OpSec” feature. We identified several 2024 and 2025 Candiru infection links to at least six domains matching Fingerprint V1 and that also contained a parameter “?q=” whose value was 16 bytes of data in Base64-encoded form. In every case, the value of the “?q=” parameter was correctly decrypted with the “V1” AES-256 key published on a page called “Ad URL OpSec Decoder” on the website myipinfo[.]io. The website myipinfo[.]io is clearly linked to Discover-Tech: passive DNS data shows multiple overlaps in IP addresses and CNAME records with other Discover-Tech websites, including powerium[.]net and myweb3id[.]io (see also Section 7).

blocks.html_en: DARK CARTOGRAPHER: Mass-Deanonymization With Ads

sentences.en: DARK CARTOGRAPHER: Mass-Deanonymization With Ads

blocks.html_en: We identified Discover-Tech ads that sought to exploit the well-known “WebRTC IP Leak” issue, which can potentially reveal the IP address of VPN and proxy users. The same ads also attempted to unmask the phone number (MSISDN) of mobile users who were served the impression. The MSISDN leaks exploit various issues, including widespread problems with so-called “zero-click login” technologies, which aim to facilitate frictionless authentication and purchases for users on their mobile devices.

sentences.en: We identified Discover-Tech ads that sought to exploit the well-known “WebRTC IP Leak” issue, which can potentially reveal the IP address of VPN and proxy users.
The same ads also attempted to unmask the phone number (MSISDN) of mobile users who were served the impression.

The MSISDN leaks exploit various issues, including widespread problems with so-called “zero-click login” technologies, which aim to facilitate frictionless authentication and purchases for users on their mobile devices.

blocks.html_en: One way “zero-click login” operates is that mobile providers select certain websites for “HTTP header enrichment,” so that when plaintext HTTP requests pass through the provider’s mobile gateway, an HTTP header (like X-MSISDN) is added to the request that provides the user’s phone number to the website. As an alternative to HTTP header enrichment, third-party services may work directly with the telco to facilitate this “zero-click login”. There appear to be widespread bugs with this allowlist matching, as well as bugs or security issues in third-party enrichment providers. While mainstream web browsers such as Chrome are moving towards blocking any non-HTTPS requests, it is likely that the app ecosystem will still embed webviews that permit non-HTTPS content.

As an alternative to HTTP header enrichment, third-party services may work directly with the telco to facilitate this “zero-click login”.
There appear to be widespread bugs with this allowlist matching, as well as bugs or security issues in third-party enrichment providers.
While mainstream web browsers such as Chrome are moving towards blocking any non-HTTPS requests, it is likely that the app ecosystem will still embed webviews that permit non-HTTPS content.

blocks.html_en: To understand the scope of Discover-Tech’s activity, we analyzed nearly four billion ad bidding records that were publicly exposed on a Discover-Tech website. We found that Discover-Tech ads were displayed in over 70,000 mobile apps, and over 120,000 websites between March and June 2026.

sentences.en: To understand the scope of Discover-Tech’s activity, we analyzed nearly four billion ad bidding records that were publicly exposed on a Discover-Tech website.
We found that Discover-Tech ads were displayed in over 70,000 mobile apps, and over 120,000 websites between March and June 2026.

blocks.html_en: We found two world-readable Apache Druid instances running on Discover-Tech’s website mtrtb[.]com. The druid.mtrtb[.]com endpoint contains bidding data for Discover-Tech’s MyDSP platform, which is connected to several upstream ad providers including Google, Yandex, Vungle, and Sunteng. The cn.druid.mtrtb[.]com endpoint appeared to contain additional bidding data for Discover-Tech’s use of Sunteng. These instances did not contain any information about Discover-Tech’s use of Beeswax or Eskimi DSPs. Discover-Tech appeared to shut down both instances in August 2026.

blocks.html_en: The database records that MyDSP spent approximately $109,091 in this period, assuming the cost is recorded in micros of USD. The database appears to be set up to record information about the revenues and profits generated by MyDSP for each ad, including fields like advertiser_revenue, dsp_profit, and margin, but these are always set to zero except for a three-day period in June where advertiser_revenue is nonzero for impressions shown for the MyIpInfo advertiser. The database also contains fields to record conversions, though these are always set to zero. A “conversion” typically refers to a purchase, app install or other action taken by a person who was exposed to an ad. It is highly unusual for an ad vendor that not a single ad leads to such an action, although it is conceivable that the bidding records might not track and record this information.

blocks.html_en: The MyDSP data shows that at least 718,748,885 of the bids (about 19%), were to show ads that apparently contained a script tag pointing to a NOAS server. We believe that the NOAS server is, generally, tasked to return some JavaScript exactly once to specific mobile ad ID and/or browser/cookie ID values, and subsequent visits return nothing until re-tasking.

sentences.en: The MyDSP data shows that at least 718,748,885 of the bids (about 19%), were to show ads that apparently contained a script tag pointing to a NOAS server.

We believe that the NOAS server is, generally, tasked to return some JavaScript exactly once to specific mobile ad ID and/or browser/cookie ID values, and subsequent visits return nothing until re-tasking.

blocks.html_en: We assessed whether an ad was likely to contain such a script tag by searching for ads whose name included the strings “infi” (a reference to Controlium’s “Infinite FIFO” feature), “NOAS”, “ppv2”, and “pqv2”. The “ppv2” and “pqv2” strings appear to be references to a newer version of the “Infinite FIFO” feature exposed as “Authenticator Manager” in the Controlium UI. We suspect that “pqv2” is for testing and/or QA, whereas “ppv2” is for production.

blocks.html_en: Ad Impression Data Highlights Systemic Risk

sentences.en: Ad Impression Data Highlights Systemic Risk

blocks.html_en: Our review of the ad bidding data indicates that Discover-Tech ads were shown on devices in national-security-sensitive networks around the world. These include the networks of various ministries of defense, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organizations and multilateral security organizations including NATO, and networks associated with critical infrastructure. The data also show impressions from the networks of media organizations around the world. At minimum, we assess that these ad impressions would have resulted in profiling by Discover-Tech. In some cases, the impressions could have resulted in code from Candiru or other entities running on the user’s device.

sentences.en: Our review of the ad bidding data indicates that Discover-Tech ads were shown on devices in national-security-sensitive networks around the world.

These include the networks of various ministries of defense, armed forces, national cyber agencies, intergovernmental organizations and multilateral security organizations including NATO, and networks associated with critical infrastructure.
The data also show impressions from the networks of media organizations around the world.
At minimum, we assess that these ad impressions would have resulted in profiling by Discover-Tech.
In some cases, the impressions could have resulted in code from Candiru or other entities running on the user’s device.

blocks.html_en: A Discover-Tech ad impression does not in and of itself confirm targeting or infection with spyware.  However, the fact that Discover-Tech was able to bid on and show ads on these networks highlights the systemic risk posed by AdFection and the advertising ecosystem, and warrants urgent investigation to determine whether any users on these networks were infected with spyware. We also note that our visibility into Discover-Tech’s impressions is confined to the data on Discover-Tech’s MyDSP platform.  This data does not include data from Beeswax and Eskimi, and covers a limited time period. This incompleteness further reinforces the need for follow-up investigation.

blocks.html_en: • In Norway, Discover-Tech ads were shown to users on the networks of the legislature (Stortinget), the Norwegian Digital Agency (Digitaliseringsdirektoratet), the Norwegian Communications Authority (Nasjonal kommunikasjonsmyndighet), state IT networks (Statens IT), the Norwegian Police (Politiets It-enhet) and serious crime units (Kripos), among many others. blocks.html_en: 6. How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the Browser

sentences.en: How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the Browser

blocks.html_en: In this section we show how, beyond targeting users of mobile apps, Discover-Tech deploys a range of techniques to deliver ads and track users while they browse across websites. This involves Discover-Tech running its own code in the user’s web browser, both while deploying ads to users and independently of showing them ads. We explore Discover-Tech’s “Banner Tester” tool to show how the company generates tracking tags and pixels attached to ads, including code that connects to a NOAS server, which we identified as a vector for spyware delivery. We also document how Discover-Tech engages in “ID syncing” with other ad vendors, and how it leverages IAB Europe’s “Transparency and Consent Framework” to appear GDPR-compliant, even while facilitating unwanted and malicious activity.

sentences.en: In this section we show how, beyond targeting users of mobile apps, Discover-Tech deploys a range of techniques to deliver ads and track users while they browse across websites.
This involves Discover-Tech running its own code in the user’s web browser, both while deploying ads to users and independently of showing them ads.

We explore Discover-Tech’s “Banner Tester” tool to show how the company generates tracking tags and pixels attached to ads, including code that connects to a NOAS server, which we identified as a vector for spyware delivery.

We also document how Discover-Tech engages in “ID syncing” with other ad vendors, and how it leverages IAB Europe’s “Transparency and Consent Framework” to appear GDPR-compliant, even while facilitating unwanted and malicious activity.

blocks.html_en: An ad displayed to a website visitor consists of an image or video to be shown and a link to be clicked, but can also carry HTML and JavaScript code that connects to one or more domains in order to track users, ad impressions, clicks, and other activities. This code is typically referred to as an ad tag. A related concept, a so-called tracking pixel, also describes code running in the web browser that connects to third-party ad vendors. Ad vendors use additional tracking code for user ID syncing by exchanging user identifiers with each other in order to identify, profile, and target website visitors across sites and vendors.

blocks.html_en: User ID Syncing with Other Ad Vendors

sentences.en: User ID Syncing with Other Ad Vendors

blocks.html_en: Unlike apps on mobile devices, web browsers do not allow websites to access a universal device identifier. The process of “ID syncing”, often also referred to as “cookie syncing”, addresses this lack of a universal user identifier. Research shows that digital advertising firms and data brokers use sophisticated forms of ID syncing to identify, profile and target web users across vendors. They achieve this by constantly exchanging user identifiers with each other, storing them in the browser and retrieving them again while users visit different websites that embed third-party tracking code.

They achieve this by constantly exchanging user identifiers with each other, storing them in the browser and retrieving them again while users visit different websites that embed third-party tracking code.

blocks.html_en: MyDSP was launched by the Israeli adtech firm Matomy in 2016. In 2018, MyDSP was “connected” to Matomy’s MobFox subsidiary, had “access” to 50 billion daily ad impressions and was able to target 500 million users, according to its website. Also in 2018, Matomy sold MyDSP to the Cypriot firm Marketcom Technologies Ltd, which belongs to the e-commerce firm Market Group owned by the Israeli billionaire Teddy Sagi, as confirmed by public filings, business data, media reporting, and whois information for the domains mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com. A 2019 version of the mydsp[.]io site confirms that MyDSP ultimately became part of Glispa, a Berlin-based adtech firm also acquired by Market Group back in 2015.

According to a Google record, the ad provider with the ID ‘3036’ changed from MarketDSP (advertising.market[.]com) to “Discover-Tech Ltd” (discover-tech[.]io) on July 31, 2020. While the company names and websites changed, the list of additional domains attributable to this Google ad provider stayed identical: (mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com).

blocks.html_en: Intelos and Its ADINT System AdHoc

sentences.en: Intelos and Its ADINT System AdHoc

blocks.html_en: In 2023, the trade press website Intelligence Online and Haaretz first reported about Intelos, a new Israeli ADINT vendor that provides a surveillance system based on data from digital advertising named “AdHoc”. Intelos was reportedly founded by Eric Banoun, who is “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel” according to Haaretz. Israeli company records reviewed by us confirm that Banoun has been a shareholder in Intelos Ltd from its registration in 2018 until present, and he is listed as the company’s director. The email address he uses in corporate filings, [email protected], clearly links Intelos Ltd to the website intelos.io.

blocks.html_en: The fact that Banoun was also listed as a director of Discover-Tech Ltd (see Section 7), already suggests a potential connection between the ADINT vendor Intelos and Discover-Tech. While we cannot assess the exact scope of the collaboration between Intelos and Discover-Tech, the technical analysis discussed in Section 4 indicates that the two work together.

blocks.html_en: On its website, Intelos purports to be a “marketing intelligence” platform that monitors “worldwide digital signals, actions, and preferences”, including “subtle changes in behaviour”, by processing 16 billion “daily data sets” across 50 countries. Much of the promotional language on the site sounds like the company’s products are built for customers in digital marketing, but could also describe an ADINT vendor. Intelos promises to “map behavioural patterns across audiences” and to build “profiles of audiences and groups” in order to “map relationships, track behavioural shifts, and anticipate collective action”. It also provides “location intelligence” based on a “proprietary index of the physical world” with “every relevant location classified, mapped, and weighted for significance”. Another system named “Nexus AI” could transform “raw data into structured insights” based on “live and historical datasets” in order to “map behavioural clusters” and “detect relationships”.

blocks.html_en: First Candiru Abuse Discoveries: 2021

sentences.en: First Candiru Abuse Discoveries: 2021

blocks.html_en: On July 15, 2021, the Citizen Lab published the first report exposing Candiru. That investigation included identifying a Candiru victim and recovering a copy of Candiru’s Windows spyware. We then worked with Microsoft’s Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC) to analyze the spyware, which led to the identification of two zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-31979 and CVE-2021-33771). We also identified over 750 websites linked to Candiru’s infection infrastructure that masqueraded as a wide range of civil society entities ranging from media organizations to Amnesty International.

The targeting we observed as part of this campaign included emails masquerading as official Spanish governmental messages about COVID.

sentences.en: Discover-Tech’s Relationship to the Digital Advertising Industry

blocks.html_en: This section explores how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, and notes that Discover-Tech achieved “certified” and “approved” status by Google and the major advertising industry association IAB Europe.

sentences.en: This section explores how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, and notes that Discover-Tech achieved “certified” and “approved” status by Google and the major advertising industry association IAB Europe.

blocks.html_en: Our analysis indicates that Discover-Tech deployed ads via Google, Yandex, and other ad vendors including Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, and Sunteng. In addition, both Google and the advertising association IAB Europe have listed Discover-Tech as a “certified” and “approved” ad vendor since the year 2020, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitate its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale.

blocks.html_en: Discover-Tech Ltd was also listed in the Global Vendor List (GVL) maintained by the European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), a key digital advertising industry association. The GVL contains roughly 1,000 vendors that are “registered and approved” by IAB Europe. These vendors can participate in IAB Europe’s “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), which promises to enable ad vendors to comply with European data protection and privacy law when processing personal data for digital advertising purposes. While the TCF’s ability to enable lawful data processing is controversially debated, a GVL registration has become a de-facto requirement for an ad vendor to participate in digital advertising, display ads and receive data in Europe. IAB Europe added Discover-Tech Ltd to the GVL on July 2, 2020. As a result of this investigation, Discover-Tech was removed from the GVL on October 8, 2026.

blocks.html_en: According to IAB Europe, it takes “reasonable steps to vet and approve” vendor applications, including the “identity of the party or parties controlling the vendor” and the vendor’s ability to “adhere” to a number of TCF policies, and then monitors their compliance with those policies. The TCF is the basis for passing user “consent” signals for personal data processing across the digital advertising supply chain, from users to publishers to intermediaries (like SSPs, DSPs, and ad exchanges) to advertisers, including in bid requests and tracking pixels. Most ad tags and tracking pixels that connect to third-party vendors require “consent” signals, including in some jurisdictions outside Europe and the U.K. like California. Google, Xandr, and most larger ad platforms require TCF compliance. While several studies found that vendors are too often ignoring “consent” signals, an ad vendor that is not listed in the GVL, and thus cannot pass any signal, can hardly interface with other ad vendors in reliable ways.

blocks.html_en: While the vendor lists maintained by Google and the IAB Europe help a company appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and are the basis to participate in the digital advertising ecosystem in a reliable way at scale, they appear to be largely based on self-attestation by vendors. They are also the basis for most of the “consent” popups shown to European web and app users every day. Discover-Tech Ltd’s inclusion in those lists potentially means that, for almost six years, hundreds of millions of Europeans were presented with a consent request that, if the recipient clicked “Agree,” could be construed as authorizing Discover-Tech to process their data under the GDPR.

sentences.en: Discussion: AdFection Shows that Online Ads Are a Cybersecurity and Privacy Crisis

blocks.html_en: This report provides the first-ever technical evidence of zero-click mercenary spyware attacks delivered via targeted advertising. We also confirm that AdFection was used to infect devices at international media organization Al Jazeera.

sentences.en: This report provides the first-ever technical evidence of zero-click mercenary spyware attacks delivered via targeted advertising.

blocks.html_en: These attacks were facilitated by Discover-Tech, which presents itself as a legitimate advertising business but actually serves as a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem. Discover-Tech not only helps companies like Candiru use ads to mass-profile unwitting phone users, their ads directly enable these companies to silently infect selected targets’ devices.

sentences.en: These attacks were facilitated by Discover-Tech, which presents itself as a legitimate advertising business but actually serves as a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem.

blocks.html_en: The combination of advertising intelligence and the delivery of spyware is extremely concerning, for several reasons. First, both the digital advertising and mercenary spyware industry are very poorly regulated, with the latter featuring numerous firms notorious for deception, a lack of transparency, and even unlawful activities. To see entities from those two industries forming an alliance should be a wakeup call to regulators and policymakers around the world. Dozens of reports by numerous organizations, including the Citizen Lab, have shown incontrovertible proof of the harms caused by mercenary spyware vendors on civil society around the globe. With the addition of the type of advertising intelligence capabilities we have documented, those firms’ capabilities will now be supercharged.

blocks.html_en: Second, the combination of advertising intelligence and spyware infections provide government security agencies with highly invasive systems that span both mass and highly targeted types of user surveillance. As we show in this report, millions of devices were likely unwittingly profiled as a form of preliminary reconnaissance to enable targeting with spyware tailored to those device’s specific characteristics. Ominously, many of these infections took place without any visible indication of tampering or other clues that might have alerted them to the compromise. Also ominous is the fact that the services of Discover-Tech appear to span multiple regions around the globe. It is not known at this time exactly which governments are capitalizing on these new capabilities, but if past evidence is any indication it seems highly likely that some proportion of them are abusing those capabilities to target individuals outside of strictly criminal or national security purposes.

sentences.en: ADINT: Journalism in the Crosshairs

blocks.html_en: The hacking of Al Jazeera with AdFection is part of a longstanding pattern: mercenary spyware attacks against the media. Journalists and newsrooms are a constant target for spyware attacks, and this latest case highlights how well-resourced operators consistently seek new ways to access their private, protected communications.

blocks.html_en: The use of spyware to target the media directly interferes with the ability of the free press to hold power to account. It also threatens the privacy of journalists’ sources, and can chill reporting. Foreknowledge of movements, reporting topics, meetings, and sources does not just help powerful interests try to frustrate coverage and reporting, it can put people at physical risk. This is especially true for a news organization with reporters, freelancers, stringers, fixers and sources working in conflict zones around the world.

blocks.html_en: Investigations into mercenary spyware operations have repeatedly surfaced targeting against the media, including in the context of governmental and cartel killings of reporters. Journalists have been confirmed spyware targets, from the Citizen Lab’s earliest findings of Pegasus spyware in Mexico almost a decade ago, to cases across Africa from Angola to Morocco and Togo, to Jordan, Serbia, El Salvador, and Italy, among many others. Organizations like Reporters Without Borders provide helpful overviews of the scale of the threat which, as Access Now points out, is sometimes coupled with laws designed to authorize government access to journalists’ communications. The International Federation of Journalists, meanwhile, has a recent overview of how spyware is situated within a broader set of digital threats against journalists.

We provide some guidance in Section 11, however we urge all news organizations to systematically review their security posture (and logs) for signs of AdFection style spyware targeting and infection.

blocks.html_en: Our findings also reveal a troubling lack of due diligence within the digital advertising industry that helped enable this inappropriate activity. Discover-Tech, which presented itself as a legitimate ad vendor but served as a bridge between the online advertising ecosystem and the spyware industry, has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the online advertising ecosystem for years. Multiple ad vendors let the company utilize their systems. The two key industry organizations, Google and IAB Europe, have helped Discover-Tech appear as a legitimate ad vendor from the year 2020 until 2026, despite information about the company’s links to figures in the spyware industry being readily accessible in corporate records. Our findings show that the digital advertising industry is ill-prepared to prevent malicious actors from exploiting its infrastructure for the distribution of spyware via targeted ads.

blocks.html_en: The AdFection attacks and espionage described in this report impact millions of people in dozens of countries. In this section, we provide guidance to regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection and ADINT-style espionage.

blocks.html_en: On October 14, 2026, we received a response from Eskimi, stating: “Eskimi has clear rules and controls designed to detect and stop advertisers who try to misuse our platform. Campaigns and creative tags are screened by independent third-party ad-verification vendors as well as by our own monitoring tools. In this case, the advertiser’s tags were built to evade automated scanning. They loaded different code depending on who was viewing the ad, including the device, IP address and location, and campaigns were often restricted to very narrow IP target lists. This is how they passed third-party verification. Our own monitoring flagged this behaviour, and campaigns and individual tags were stopped as our controls detected them. We have since shared the relevant technical indicators with our supply partners. In the interest of supporting your research, the indicators we identified include creative tags calling remote “getAd” loaders hosted on dtech.adtimizer.co, several mtrtb.com subdomains (noas, infinoas and ppv2), and events.myweb3id.io. Because these loaders served different code depending on the viewer and targeting, they were not detected by third-party ad-verification scanning. Additional technical information can be provided where it is useful for your research. Discover-Tech had been a self-service advertiser on the Eskimi DSP since 2022, under our standard advertiser terms. Because of our campaign and individual tag blocks, its activity remained small, amounting to only a few hundred dollars in media spend. Its last campaign through the Eskimi DSP was stopped on 6 August 2026, and no impressions have been served since. Once the full pattern of the advertiser’s behaviour became clear, we permanently blocked all of its accounts, users and associated domains. We are working with independent ad-security specialists to help identify similar behaviour across the industry. As I mentioned, happy to contribute with anything that can help with further investigation and ensuring compliance in the ad-tech market.”

sentences.en: On October 14, 2026, we received a response from Eskimi, stating: “Eskimi has clear rules and controls designed to detect and stop advertisers who try to misuse our platform.
Campaigns and creative tags are screened by independent third-party ad-verification vendors as well as by our own monitoring tools.
In this case, the advertiser’s tags were built to evade automated scanning.
They loaded different code depending on who was viewing the ad, including the device, IP address and location, and campaigns were often restricted to very narrow IP target lists.
This is how they passed third-party verification.
Our own monitoring flagged this behaviour, and campaigns and individual tags were stopped as our controls detected them.
We have since shared the relevant technical indicators with our supply partners.

In the interest of supporting your research, the indicators we identified include creative tags calling remote “getAd” loaders hosted on dtech.adtimizer.co, several mtrtb.com subdomains (noas, infinoas and ppv2), and events.myweb3id.io.
Because these loaders served different code depending on the viewer and targeting, they were not detected by third-party ad-verification scanning.
Additional technical information can be provided where it is useful for your research.
Discover-Tech had been a self-service advertiser on the Eskimi DSP since 2022, under our standard advertiser terms.
Because of our campaign and individual tag blocks, its activity remained small, amounting to only a few hundred dollars in media spend.
Its last campaign through the Eskimi DSP was stopped on 6 August 2026, and no impressions have been served since.
Once the full pattern of the advertiser’s behaviour became clear, we permanently blocked all of its accounts, users and associated domains.
We are working with independent ad-security specialists to help identify similar behaviour across the industry.
As I mentioned, happy to contribute with anything that can help with further investigation and ensuring compliance in the ad-tech market.”

sentences.en: Appendix B.
Glossary

blocks.html_en: Adtech vendor, ad vendor. Advertising technology intermediary such as a Demand-Side Platform (DSP), Supply-Side Platform (SSP) (both defined below) or ad exchange.

sentences.en: Adtech vendor, ad vendor.
Advertising technology intermediary such as a Demand-Side Platform (DSP), Supply-Side Platform (SSP) (both defined below) or ad exchange.

blocks.html_en: Ad Slot. Designated space or position on a website or mobile app reserved to display an ad.

sentences.en: Ad Slot.
Designated space or position on a website or mobile app reserved to display an ad.

blocks.html_en: Demand-Side Platform (DSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps advertisers buy ad placements across many different websites or mobile apps in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by ad exchanges.

sentences.en: Demand-Side Platform (DSP).

System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps advertisers buy ad placements across many different websites or mobile apps in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by ad exchanges.

blocks.html_en: Supply-Side Platform (SSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps publishers of websites or mobile apps sell ad slots in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by an ad exchange, which is often operated by the same ad vendor as the SSP.

sentences.en: Supply-Side Platform (SSP).

System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps publishers of websites or mobile apps sell ad slots in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by an ad exchange, which is often operated by the same ad vendor as the SSP.

blocks.html_en: Ad Exchange. Automated marketplace operated by an adtech intermediary that hosts real-time auctions which facilitate the selling of ad slots and the buying of ad placements across many publishers, advertisers and intermediaries like DSPs and SSPs. Ad exchanges are often operated by SSPs.

sentences.en: Ad Exchange.

Automated marketplace operated by an adtech intermediary that hosts real-time auctions which facilitate the selling of ad slots and the buying of ad placements across many publishers, advertisers and intermediaries like DSPs and SSPs.
Ad exchanges are often operated by SSPs.

blocks.html_en: Real-Time Bidding (RTB). Automated high-frequency auctions hosted by ad exchanges where advertisers (or DSPs on their behalf) bid on ad placements offered by website and mobile app publishers (or their SSPs). When a user visits a website or uses an app that sells targeted ads via RTB, the publisher’s SSP initiates a bid request that transmits data about the user and the ad slot to several DSPs, who submit bids on behalf of advertisers. The ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user.

sentences.en: Real-Time Bidding (RTB).
Automated high-frequency auctions hosted by ad exchanges where advertisers (or DSPs on their behalf) bid on ad placements offered by website and mobile app publishers (or their SSPs).

When a user visits a website or uses an app that sells targeted ads via RTB, the publisher’s SSP initiates a bid request that transmits data about the user and the ad slot to several DSPs, who submit bids on behalf of advertisers.
The ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user.

blocks.html_en: Bid Request. RTB auction record that describes an ad slot and the user who currently visits a website or uses a mobile app. Bid requests are initiated by publishers and sent via an SSP and an ad exchange to several DSPs, which place bids in order to show ads to specific users on behalf of advertisers. Bid requests typically contain personal data about users in order to facilitate targeted advertising.

sentences.en: Bid Request.
RTB auction record that describes an ad slot and the user who currently visits a website or uses a mobile app.
Bid requests are initiated by publishers and sent via an SSP and an ad exchange to several DSPs, which place bids in order to show ads to specific users on behalf of advertisers.

blocks.html_en: Mobile Advertising ID (MAID). Unique identifier for a mobile device used for advertising and tracking purposes, assigned by the device’s operating system such as Google Android or Apple iOS. While users can reset or delete mobile ad IDs in the settings, they are activated by default. Advertising and data companies use mobile ad IDs to link user data across contexts and vendors in order to track, follow, profile and target users.
